cards.title: AI-first support routing, then human training
cards.summary: Use AI-first customer-service software to bucket and route tickets to the best-fit rep, then back it with core-values training and hands-on leader coaching.
cards.use_when: Choosing or upgrading your store's helpdesk/support stack, or fixing slow or inconsistent responses to pre-purchase and post-purchase tickets.
steps: Adopt an AI-first support platform whose primary job is to classify and route the query to the correct human (product, shipping, or other), not to resolve the whole interaction autonomously. The source describes this bucketing-to-right-rep step as the biggest early lever.

Survey actual operators you trust about which platform is currently best — the source notes the tooling changes so fast it must be revisited, and operator peer recommendations drove their switches. Verify current product names and capabilities before committing.
Do not assume every rep is equivalent: the source observes a large quality delta between best and worst support staff, so routing and staffing decisions matter more than average response time.

Write down how your team deals with customers (a 'customer service bible') and train new hires hands-on against core values early, with a team leader working closely with them in their first weeks rather than leaving onboarding to documentation alone.
caveats: Tool recommendations in the source are dated and specific to one brand's stack; re-evaluate before adopting.
AI routing only helps if the underlying human teams are trained and staffed.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Membership club as LTV engine and research panel
cards.summary: A paid membership aggregates your highest-LTV customers, then a smaller opt-in community channel turns them into a feedback and product-innovation panel.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviving a loyalty/membership program, or setting up a customer community to source product ideas and merchandising feedback.
steps: Offer obvious member benefits first (the source cites 20% savings and free shipping) to build the base of invested, repeat buyers.

Expect a small hardcore subset to opt into the engagement channel: the source had ~100,000 active members but only ~5,000 in the Facebook group. Treat that 5,000 as your true-fan panel and put the product team in the room with them.

Mine the panel for specific asks (for example, a 36-inch inseam or a new style variant) and answer concretely, including timelines when you can. The source reports members suggesting a product a year before it launched.
Validate a single member's idea across the broader group ('does this affect you too?') before acting, so one loud opinion doesn't drive roadmap decisions.
Close the loop publicly when you ship something a member suggested — the source argues this makes members evangelists who police your retail displays and keep engaging.
Use the club to recruit your highest-value repeat customers first, then invite them downfunnel into the community.
caveats: Membership is a long-horizon LTV play; the source calls it an LTV game changer, not a fast acquisition tactic.
The 100k/5k ratio is one brand's example, not a benchmark; engagement rates vary by category.
Requires real product-team access and willingness to say no or not-yet honestly.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Choose the KPI window and stop intraday panic
cards.summary: Lean on blended ROAS, new-customer CAC, CPMs and channel-level ROAS, but judge strategy on a monthly-to-yearly window and P&L netting rather than daily swings.
cards.use_when: Setting your store's KPI dashboard and deciding when a performance dip actually warrants intervention.
steps: Track blended ROAS (all revenue against all cost) as the top-line operating health check, plus new-customer acquisition ROAS, new-customer CAC, and CPMs. The source notes CPMs spiked during an election period, so treat them as an external variable to watch, not an internal failure.
Compare channel ROAS week over week across Meta, Google/YouTube, TikTok and others to see who is improving or degrading relative to each other.
Separate 'business is fine today' from 'the strategy is working': the source notes blended ROAS can flip mid-day simply because an email went out at noon, which tells you nothing about strategy.

The source admits to unhealthy intraday obsession and says the healthier frame is monthly, ideally yearly, especially during a deliberate strategic transition. When you make a big spend-mix change, commit to judging the business week-over-week on unit economics and P&L, not on daily ROAS.
Avoid the founder pattern of reacting schizophrenically to one or two down weeks — this is the source's described correction to their own early behavior.
caveats: Monthly windows are the source's stated preference, not a universal rule; how long you can stomach a dip depends on your cash position and the bet's scale.
Blended ROAS can look good because of late-day retention sends rather than acquisition health.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Levers when ROAS drops: retention before discounts
cards.summary: When performance softens, the source's first lever is retention — more email/SMS sends, better flows — not immediately reaching for discounts.
cards.use_when: Responding to a week of below-target ROAS or CAC, or when planning your quarterly growth lever stack.
steps: Prioritize retention over acquisition: the source states the repeat business drives the whole thing and that growth by leaps and bounds comes from figuring out retention.

Build and maintain the core automated flows: welcome flow, funnel flows, abandoned-cart recoveries. The source says the welcome flow is the most important touchpoint because that is where the customer decides whether to try you.
Send more emails and SMSs and find ways to bring people back to the site before discounting, which is the first-time-entrepreneur reflex the interviewer named and the source did not endorse.
Hire a dedicated retention leader early: the source says you cannot invest enough time in getting a retention owner into the business to build those flows.
caveats: The source explicitly warns 'stay off the discount crackpipe' — deeper discounting as a default lever erodes margin and trains discount-waiting.
Requires list size and consent assets; without them retention sends have limited reach.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Optimize the welcome flow offer with stepwise tests
cards.summary: Test the welcome-flow first-purchase incentive in deliberate increments and stop where lift flattens; the source found 20% off was the sweet spot versus 10% and 30%.
cards.use_when: Setting or revising your first-purchase incentive and welcome-flow structure to lift new-customer conversion.
steps: Start higher than you might instinctively: the source moved the welcome offer from 10% to 20% and calls the revenue lift astronomical, and regrets starting at 10%.

Test the next increment before committing to it: 20% to 30% produced no additional lift for the source, so they reverted to 20% and held it. Treat this as one brand's tested outcome, not a universal benchmark for your category.
State the brand's value proposition clearly in that first email — the source says the welcome email is where customers decide whether to adopt your product, so it must communicate what you stand for.
Put a free-shipping offer in a later welcome-flow email (the source uses the third) to neutralize the 'everything ships free' objection on its own timeline rather than leading with it.
Run a longer-horizon 'hail mary': the source offers a deeper discount to welcome-flow subscribers who still haven't purchased after ~120 days, to test whether they are a viable customer.
Consider replacing percentage-off with cash-back if your platform supports it; the source reports that transition worked well for them via a cash-back provider.
caveats: 20% as the sweet spot is source-specific and category-dependent — verify with your own sequential tests.
Discount depth interacts with AOV and margin; pair this with AOV work rather than treating the offer as standalone.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Treat creative quality as the acquisition differentiator
cards.summary: With broad-targeting ad platforms, creative quality is the main lever; hold content to an internal bar before spending behind it.
cards.use_when: Reviewing ad creative before launch, deciding whether to keep an agency or build in-house, or diagnosing why broad-targeted spend underperforms.
steps: Set an explicit internal quality bar and enforce it before the market sees anything. The source's stated bar is an 8/10, arguing you must be honest internally about a 4/10 instead of rationalizing it.
Have the hard internal conversation when creative misses, without crushing the maker's confidence — the source frames this honesty-for-the-customer as a required leadership behavior.
Iterate to a completely different endpoint: the source cites the TubeScience model of starting in one place and ending in another through repeated testing and re-iteration.
If an agency returns a 6/10, weigh whether your internal team can raise it to an 8/10 — the source reports doing exactly that and concludes you should build the internal talent muscle.

Remember the platform no longer rescues weak content: the source argues broad targeting means everyone is shown everything, so 'how good you can do on your side creative-wise' is the only differentiator.

For acquisition creative, direct-response UGC and value-prop ads were ~90% of the source's spend before a brand push, so treat selling-content and comedy/brand-content as distinct mixes to allocate deliberately.
caveats: The 8/10 bar is the source's subjective standard, not a measured threshold.
The 90/10 creative mix is one brand's historic allocation and was being deliberately changed — it is not a recommended default.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Price and merchandise in packs to raise AOV
cards.summary: Bundle multi-packs and a pack-builder so customers get a discount off single-unit MSRP, which the source says is how they lifted AOV from $36 to $112.
cards.use_when: Deciding PDP or collection merchandising structure (singles vs packs), or building a pack-builder and pricing ladder to raise AOV.
steps: Default to packs rather than singles. The source argues charging full price for one unit is not doing right by the customer — lump items into packs so they receive a genuine discount off the suggested retail price.
Offer a pack-builder so customers who want to choose their own assortment can do so; the source credits this with driving AOV and product mix.
Watch the AOV math: the source attributes their $36-to-$112 AOV move to conversion-rate optimization work including pack structure, not to a single tactic.

Accept short-term tradeoffs for a better cart mix: the source removed PDP breadcrumb navigation that let shoppers leave to browse categories, took the revenue loss, and kept better product-mix behavior because it preferred guiding customers to what they came for.
caveats: Pack pricing must keep per-unit margin viable; discounting off MSRP is not automatically profitable.
The $36-to-$112 figure is one brand's result over time, not a benchmark or promised outcome.
The breadcrumb decision is a stated preference for product mix over short-term revenue — evaluate against your own category's browse behavior.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Design the cart as the highest-leverage CRO surface
cards.summary: Put the most impactful conversion and AOV work in the cart, including tiered gift-with-purchase thresholds, and make the experience feel rewarding.
cards.use_when: Redesigning cart and checkout, setting free-shipping and gift thresholds, or planning your conversion-optimization roadmap priorities.
steps: Set tiered cart thresholds with progressively better gifts: the source's example is free shipping at ~$100, a free shirt at ~$150, free joggers at ~$200.
Use gifts to introduce new categories: a t-shirt buyer who hits $150 receives an activewear tee and may return to buy the activewear line they'd never have tried.

Consider a rewards-feeling mechanic at checkout rather than an ordinary add-on. The source wanted it to feel like winning something, and got pushback on a literal slot machine — so the goal is the feeling, not the specific gimmick.

One example of a gamified mechanic: a sports-event parlay page where participants pick outcomes, win store credit, and the first ~1,000 players are gifted — used to drive traffic that previously went to social.
Treat CRO as one continuous split-test program across the whole site, with the cart as the place to obsess most.
caveats: Threshold dollar amounts are the source's chosen example levels, not derived benchmarks; set yours from your own AOV and margin.
Gift-with-purchase adds fulfillment cost and inventory consumption — model the margin impact.
Gamified mechanics can read as gimmicky; the source explicitly narrowed their own idea after feedback.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Change one variable per test in CRO
cards.summary: Run conversion experiments sequentially, changing one element at a time, because rolling out multiple changes at once makes attribution impossible.
cards.use_when: Planning site A/B tests or interpreting a test that produced an unexpected result.
steps: Do not ship four changes simultaneously. The source and interviewer both name this as the biggest split-testing mistake: you lose the ability to tell which change moved the number.
When a multi-change rollout fails, revert to the drawing board and isolate one change at a time to find the culprit.
Accept that strong intuition still loses: the source says they make bets with good intuition that don't work, so plan for re-testing rather than assuming.
Use a testing tool such as Intelligence (verify current name and interface) and staff the program, since the source says the work must be actively run, not set and forget.
Keep a record of which single change produced which result so learning compounds across the site.
caveats: Single-variable discipline is slower; the source treats that cost as acceptable versus unusable results.
Tooling named in the source may have changed — confirm before purchase.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Simplify the homepage and PDP like a landing page
cards.summary: Strip the site toward first principles, because heatmaps show most visitors don't scroll past the fold, and treat the homepage as a concise funnel.
cards.use_when: Rebuilding the homepage or PDP, deciding how much content and navigation to include above and below the fold.
steps: Run heatmap testing and look honestly at what gets seen. The source states nobody scrolls past the fold, so all the beautiful content below it is largely unseen.
Adopt a zero-based-budget mindset for the page: start with a blank screen and add back only what you truly need (a product, minimal upsells and animations), rather than what each internal team wants.
Simplify the PDP aggressively: the source reports overhauling their PDP and seeing a game-changing revenue increase, which then motivated simplifying the homepage too.
Make the homepage concise and funnel-like, hitting core value propositions without being too long or too short.
Use the source's benchmark for over-simplification: Zara's site feels like browsing a white room with no obvious product — the source admires the first-principles approach but notes it as an extreme.
caveats: The fold claim is the source's read of their own heatmaps; test your own site and traffic mix.
Aggressive simplification is a preference with real tradeoffs — some brands, and the source itself, still use lifestyle creative on PDPs.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Sell value with side-by-side visuals on homepage and retail displays
cards.summary: Show why to buy via side-by-side comparison imagery instead of only aspirational lifestyle shots, and carry that story into retail display units.
cards.use_when: Planning hero and homepage imagery, PDP creative, or designing a retail display that must tell the product story without a screen.
steps: Lead with the customer's actual question — 'why should I buy this?' — using side-by-side comparisons on the homepage. The source calls this atypical versus the standard 'cool guy in the park' shot.
Keep a balance: the source still uses lifestyle creative in PDPs, so use side-by-sides where the buying decision happens and lifestyle where it supports.

For wholesale/retail, translate the same side-by-side story onto the display unit. The source says this was the hardest part of retail and told partners that the display must carry the story or it won't work.
Use the display as the content in environments you don't control — the source's Target rollout performed well once the display told the story properly.
caveats: Side-by-side comparison claims must be accurate and defensible in advertising.
The source's retail display success is one brand's rollout, not a guarantee for other categories.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Run post-purchase surveys as your attribution truth source
cards.summary: Use post-purchase survey responses to check whether platform-reported attribution matches where customers say they came from, and diversify spend accordingly.
cards.use_when: Auditing ad-channel mix, reconciling platform ROAS against actual profitability, or deciding where to shift budget.
steps: Install a post-purchase survey tool (source example: No Commerce — verify current product and interface) so every buyer answers where they first heard about you.

Set the expectation check: if roughly half your spend is on Meta, roughly half of survey responses should attribute to Meta. The source frames a mismatch as evidence you're spending into a black hole.
Trust the survey over in-platform attribution when the two conflict. The source argues platforms over-attribute and the survey reflects what actual customers say at scale.
Use survey data to rebalance the mix rather than to celebrate flattering in-platform ROAS: the source describes seeing great Facebook ROAS while company profitability didn't net out.
Use trending survey responses to judge upper-funnel brand investments that are otherwise untrackable, including live events and sponsorships.
caveats: Survey attribution is self-reported and recall-based; use it as a triangulation source, not a perfect ledger.
The '40% of spend should show ~40% of responses' rule is the source's sanity-check heuristic, not a formal calculation.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Post-purchase upsell with staffed, intelligent offers
cards.summary: A post-purchase one-click upsell can add meaningful net profit, but only if someone actively curates what is shown to whom.
cards.use_when: Setting up post-purchase upsell offers at checkout, or deciding whether the upsell app can be left unattended.
steps: Use a post-purchase upsell app that presents an additional offer after payment is authorized (source example: AfterSell — verify current features), so acceptance is one click and the card is already charged.

Do not set and forget. The source says the app was underused until one dedicated person obsessed over it; that person's work took it from a few hundred thousand a year to multi-millions in pure profit.

Show contextually relevant products: use logic that accounts for what is already in the cart so the offer is native to the purchase. If a customer buys one item, offer more of that item at a larger discount with specialized pricing.
Staff the role with someone who combines data analysis, marketing understanding and consumer insight, then sense-check their decisions after the fact.
Treat the upsell as pure margin: the customer is already acquired, so the source counts this as straight-to-bottom-line profit.
caveats: The source's 'could very easily account for 5-10-15% of net profit' is their observed range for their business, not a guaranteed return.
The multi-million result followed dedicated staffing — expect much less from an unattended install.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Allocate spend with platforms over-attributing and creative degrading
cards.summary: Spread budget across Meta, Google/YouTube, TikTok and newer networks, but base the split on survey truth rather than platform dashboards, and re-test channels as they change.
cards.use_when: Planning channel budget allocation or evaluating a new ad network for your store.
steps: Use a rough starting shape from the source's mix as an example only: around 50% Meta, roughly 15-20% Google and YouTube combined, with the rest across other channels.

Test emerging networks seriously. The source reports AppLovin surprising them by competing at Facebook-level spend efficiency, driven notably by a middle-aged-female cohort buying for the men in their lives — and flags that Q4 performance may not hold in Q1/Q2, so keep testing.
Recognize platform limitations: the source says Meta's algorithm no longer rescues weak creative and that the media-buying era is largely over, shifting the burden to your own content quality.

Keep TikTok in perspective: the source spends five figures a day there without crushing it, and sees the platform favoring beauty and fashion; they expect it to work better once they launch a women's line.
Add later-stage channels once the core three are working — TV worked for the source because their creative is long-form, and podcast ad reads suit brands with comics who can speak honestly at length.
Verify current network capabilities and pricing before reallocating — the source notes the landscape moves fast.
caveats: The percentage mix is one brand's allocation with an $80M+/year budget; smaller advertisers should not copy proportions.
AppLovin's Q4 performance may have been seasonal — the source itself questions whether it holds outside Q4.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Buy live-event brand deals for fan moments, not logos
cards.summary: When evaluating sponsorships, refuse static logo placements and pay only for experiences that create emotional connection with attending fans.
cards.use_when: Negotiating or evaluating a team/franchise sponsorship, stadium placement or live-event brand deal.
steps: Challenge proposals that price static splashy assets (on-ice logo etchings, court vinyl, jersey logos). The source calls these massively overpriced for the value delivered, and notes jersey logos run multiple millions per team per year.

Use trigger events as the model: something that happens in the game unlocks a giveaway for everyone, similar to a free-throw promotion where a missed free throw earns fans a free item. The source wants to build these for their brand.

Direct the budget into fan-facing moments — giveaways, seat upgrades, moving a fan from the top row to the front row, or surprising someone who wasn't at the game at all. The source calls it making a lifelong fan through an unexpected moment.

Look at what already works in-venue: the source observed gamified fan interactions on the jumbotron where the crowd rooted for participants, and wants to build a game where everyone wins something, not just the players.
Set the expectation of untrackability: the source says you must give up some measurement because these are upper-funnel plays, though strong ones should show up in post-purchase surveys.
Budget realistically: the source says six figures minimum to work with these organizations, easily seven, with on-court/on-field placements at hundreds of thousands.
caveats: The source admits this is new and expensive territory for them and that they are learning what works the hard way.
Requires accepting weak direct attribution; if you cannot tolerate that, stay in trackable channels.
The source explicitly says they are not with overspending when that money could go to attributable Facebook spend.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Keep opex lean via revenue per employee
cards.summary: Track revenue per employee and keep OPEX low by hiring few, elite generalists rather than staffing up, so you can stay profitable without primary fundraising.
cards.use_when: Making hiring decisions, planning org structure during a growth phase, or deciding whether to raise capital for operating expenses.
steps: Watch revenue per employee and total OPEX deliberately and early — the source calls it incredibly important and credits it with never needing to raise primary capital.
Hire killers: the source's approach is to bring in A-level talent who can do the work of ten people rather than hiring ten people, which directly lowers OPEX.
Prefer generalist operator/entrepreneur DNA in leaders early. The source says these hires save money because you no longer need the headcount you assumed.
Expect elite hires to demand elite peers: the source says the strongest people push back and ask for higher-caliber colleagues, so a mixed roster creates retention risk.

Do the work yourself early. The source is blunt that founders must do everything for a stretch and can't hire their way to comfort, and that no fancy office is warranted until revenue and profitability sustain the overhead — start from an apartment if needed.
Note that lenders still underwrite on OPEX, so a lean cost base strengthens your position if you later want debt-based growth capital.
caveats: Extreme leanness is a strategic preference with burnout risk; the source acknowledges it means a hard couple of years.
Not raising primary equity is not the same as raising nothing — the source mentions secondary sales, debt and revolving credit lines as alternatives.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Fund growth with supplier terms before debt or equity
cards.summary: Push out net terms with manufacturers as the first financing lever, then negotiate revolving credit once you have proven scale.
cards.use_when: Managing cash flow for inventory purchasing, or deciding how to finance a large inventory or category bet.
steps: Start with your production partner, where the source says you have the most leverage, and negotiate payment terms before considering a credit facility.
Expect to earn terms progressively: the source describes starting with money upfront, then 15-day, 30-day, 45-day terms, and rarely 90-180 days with very strong partners.

Negotiate terms by telling the growth story — for example, 'we're doing $15M and will do $90M next year, do you want that business?' — and then actually deliver the volume, because the terms depend on credibility.
Once established, ask for a revolving credit line for large category bets; the source's example is a $25M revolver where the supplier floats raw materials and you pay against specific SKUs.
Honor terms. The source states that going over agreed terms means interest or another form of compensation, and that you must figure something out with the supplier.

Assess debt honestly before taking it: the source says the biggest mistake is borrowing when you aren't confident the business works, and notes lenders like Wayflyer decline most applicants and require connected financial data.
caveats: The specific term lengths and credit amounts are the source's experience at scale ($80M+ spend) and won't be offered to new sellers.
Attribution of revenue growth to supplier terms is the source's account, not a measurable benchmark.
Verify any lender's current underwriting process and integrations before applying.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Open stores for foot traffic, not density
cards.summary: Site retail leases inside high-traffic malls even at high rent, avoid standalone stores, and accept store P&L near break-even as an upper-funnel cost.
cards.use_when: Selecting a retail location, evaluating lease economics, or deciding whether brick-and-mortar fits your brand.
steps: Prioritize mall foot traffic over customer density. The source says their standalone stores in prime locations lost a lot of money because destinations require customers to make a special trip.
Budget for expensive leases: the source cites $20,000-$40,000 per month for high-traffic mall space, and says you should be ready for the P&L not to look pretty at first.

Target break-even in four walls and attribute the rest to top-of-funnel value — store signage in a mall is constant visual brand exposure and lets customers see and touch product. The source reports some stores profitable immediately where traffic and demo density were high (Mall of America, Florida).
Take smaller spaces to get into great malls: the source's stores are roughly 1,000-1,500 sq ft, which is tight but worth it for the location.
Use an operator-partner model to test before committing capex: the source started with Leap, which staffs the store and takes on many costs, and recommends it for testing one or two stores.
Verify whether retail brand exposure is working via post-purchase survey responses naming the store.
caveats: Retail economics depend heavily on local rent; the source's numbers are their markets and won't transfer directly.
Store-as-funnel logic is deliberately accepting weak direct attribution — the source's stated view, not a universal rule.
The source describes learning retail by doing it wrong first, including costly standalone leases.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Sequence retail entry after digital proof
cards.summary: The source's Target deal began as a digital marketplace integration and roll-out test, and their advice to others is to build digital volume first, then expand into wholesale.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a wholesale or marketplace partnership, or deciding when to approach a large retailer.
steps: Start with a digital marketplace integration before physical shelf space. The source describes integrating their Shopify catalog so Target purchases ship directly to Target customers, then running a test, then a roll-out that sold through and earned reorders and assortment expansion.
Use the test-then-roll-out structure: prove sell-through on a limited assortment before negotiating broader placement.
Fight for control of the in-store display, because the side-by-side product story is how the brand converts — the source told the retailer that without the right display, the story couldn't be told.

If you're a digital-first brand, accept that wholesale is unfamiliar and be patient: the source had no retail expertise, and their late entry came from discomfort rather than strategy — they acknowledge they'd have started earlier if they'd known retail.
Expect the retail relationship to be driven by people and integrations as much as by metrics; the source's opportunity came through an executive relationship and a platform integration.
caveats: The Target partnership details are unique to that relationship and timeline — treat them as an example of a sequence, not a playbook you can request.
Increased wholesale volume adds assortment, replenishment and display obligations you must resource.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx
